title: The work, not the fruit
hookLine: the word Gandhi put on the cover: anasakti
carry: your right is to the work, not its fruit

lines: ONE VERSE IN THE SECOND CHAPTER.
cards: Arjuna stands between the two armies with his bow on the ground. He can see how this might end: teachers dead, cousins dead, a kingdom won and nothing worth having in it. Fear of the outcome has frozen him.
In the second chapter, Krishna's answer holds one of the best-known verses in the whole Gita. When Gandhi made his own Gita in Gujarati, he didn't name it after Krishna or after the battle.
He named it after the idea in that verse.

teach.h: ANASAKTI: NOT CLINGING TO THE FRUIT.
teach.b: The title is Anasakti Yoga. Anasakti is usually put into English as non-attachment, or selfless action: doing the work without clinging to what it gets you.
Gandhi said this was the Gita's central teaching, the one the rest of the book circles around.

teach.h: YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK ALONE.
teach.b: It's gathered in that verse, where Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And don't cling to doing nothing, either.
That last part closes the easy exit. Letting go of the fruit is not walking away from the field.
Many Hindu families know it by its opening words, karmanye vadhikaraste; it's a verse grandparents still quote before a big exam. Gandhi pushed against a misreading here.

teach.h: LETTING GO IS NOT NOT CARING.
teach.b: Non-attachment, he wrote, doesn't mean not caring how things turn out. The one who lets go of the fruit is wholly given to doing the task well, because nothing is being saved up for the reward.
In a little book called Hind Swaraj, he had a picture for this.

teach.h: THE MEANS ARE A SEED, THE END A TREE.
teach.b: The means are like a seed, and the end like a tree. You can't plant one kind of seed and expect another kind of tree. So if you care about the end, care first about the means, the part actually in your hands.
Now Arjuna's freeze makes sense. He can't control how the war ends. He can do his part, with full care.

teach.h: THE WORK IS YOURS. LET THE FRUIT GO.
teach.b: Anasakti is exactly that: the work given wholly, the fruit let go.

how: Some who follow the Gita's path of action try to offer their daily work without clinging to its results, and some readers of Gandhi pair Gita 2:47 with his line that means and ends are like seed and tree.

o: the Gita read as work given fully, its fruit let go
a Gita that promises rich rewards for those who work hard
a Gita that tells readers to stop working and withdraw

games.q: the word on the cover — tap the pairs.

s: for Gandhi, non-attachment means not caring how things turn out
he wrote the opposite: the one who lets go of the fruit gives full attention to doing the task well.
the Gita verse Gandhi leaned on also warns against clinging to doing nothing
your right is to the work alone, not its fruits; and don't cling to inaction either.
in Hind Swaraj, Gandhi says the end justifies whatever means it takes
he pictured the means as a seed and the end as a tree: what you plant decides what grows.

games.q: you're working hard for a good result you may never see. the work is slow and no one's watching. what does Gandhi's Gita ask of you?
o: stop, since the result is out of your hands.
do this step well, and let the result go.
work only on what pays off quickly.
games.why: anasakti: your right is to the work alone, never its fruits, and not to doing nothing either. Gandhi said letting go of the fruit frees attention for the work itself.

practice: Pick one thing you're working on, a project, a conversation you hope goes well, a person you're trying to help, and notice how much of your mind is already standing at the finish line.

Walk it gently back to the one small step in your hands today, and on each out-breath set the result down, like a bag you've been carrying. If you pray, you can offer the work, and its fruit, to Krishna, or to the one you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi's Gita. He called it Anasakti Yoga: the work given fully, the fruit let go.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: anasakti, non-attachment; the word Gandhi chose for the title of his Gita.

carryVoice: Your line: your right is to the work, not its fruit. Tomorrow, how a wise person walks. See you then.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2:47 (the right to the work, not its fruits; no clinging to inaction)
Anasakti Yoga, Gandhi's introduction (renunciation of fruit as the Gita's central teaching; not indifference to the result)
Hind Swaraj, the chapter on brute force (means as seed, end as tree)
